claims.text: Retention of high toughness in severely deformed high-entropy alloys is governed by a narrow post-processing treatment window.
Within the optimal treatment window, residual stress can be relieved without triggering deleterious grain-boundary precipitation.
Severe deformation such as cold rolling or forging produces a high density of dislocations in the alloy.
Severe deformation leaves substantial residual stresses in the alloy.
Recovery processes compete with precipitation kinetics over the proposed annealing range.
Grain-boundary segregation and precipitate formation or suppression mediate the toughness response.
Grain-boundary precipitates can act as crack-initiation sites.
Moderate heat treatment relieves dislocation-induced stresses.
Moderate heat treatment refines the grain-boundary structure.
Stress relief and grain-boundary refinement improve toughness by enabling ductile deformation.
Excessive heat treatment accelerates the precipitation of brittle intermetallic phases at grain boundaries.
Brittle grain-boundary intermetallic phases reduce toughness through intergranular embrittlement.
Annealing within the optimal treatment window will produce greater toughness than the as-processed baseline.
Over-annealing will produce lower toughness than annealing within the optimal treatment window.
The proposed behavior applies to severely plastically deformed, multi-principal-element high-entropy alloys before complete recrystallization or extensive phase transformation occurs.
The location of the treatment window and the magnitude of the toughness response vary with alloy composition and processing history.
